case_studies.title: AIGen: Automating AI Bill of Materials Generation Through Hybrid MLOps Integration
case_studies.abstract: The responsible development and deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) systems requires rigorous documentation of their constituent artifacts, e.g., datasets, model weights, training pipelines, and runtime dependencies. Although the Software Package Data Exchange (SPDX) 3.0 standard introduced native support for AI and dataset profiles, practical tooling capable of generating standards-compliant AI Bills of Materials (AIBoMs) in an automated and extensible manner remains scarce. This paper presents AIGen, a modular AIBoM generator that produces machine-readable, interoperable inventories o
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of manually documenting AI system components by building AIGen, a tool that automates the generation of AI Bills of Materials. AIGen produces machine-readable inventories of AI system artifacts, making it easier to track and manage AI deployments. The result is a more streamlined and compliant AI development process.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI or machine learning infrastructure, here is what to do: review your current documentation process, consider integrating AIGen to automate AIBoM generation, and ensure compliance with the SPDX 3.0 standard. This flags a risk: if your org uses AI systems without proper documentation, check your audit and compliance processes immediately.
case_studies.relevance_tag: AIBoM, Hybrid MLOps, AI deployment, Extensibility
case_studies.score_reasoning: High novelty in the context of AIBoM generation, which is relevant to IT engineers working with AI deployments. The system's extensibility and modularity could be valuable in real-world applications within 90 days, making it worth considering for IT engineers and consultants.

case_studies.title: When Derived Measurements Mislead: Quantifying and Mitigating LLM Over-Trust with Privileged-Modality Reliability Evidence
case_studies.abstract: Derived measurements increasingly enter large language model (LLM) pipelines as direct facts despite their instance-dependent validity. We define derived-feature over-trust (DFOT) as the failure in which a downstream LLM assigns such a measurement the epistemic status of a direct fact or uses it outside its valid scope. Using physiological sensing as a case study, D1 tests acceptance of a PPG-derived rhythm contradicted by offline ECG, whereas D2 tests rejection of an offline-confirmed reliable PPG rhythm under misleading severe history. ECG supplies training supervision and offline reference
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of over-trusting derived measurements in large language models, where the team built a system to quantify and mitigate this issue using physiological sensing as a case study, resulting in a better understanding of how to avoid assigning incorrect epistemic status to derived measurements. The study used ECG and PPG-derived rhythm to test acceptance and rejection of reliable and contradictory data. This research does not directly affect cloud infrastructure management work.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on the trustworthiness of derived measurements in large language models, which is more relevant to AI and machine learning applications rather than cloud infrastructure management. If your organization uses large language models, this research may be of interest to the AI or data science teams. However, it does not require immediate attention from IT infrastructure managers.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty: 10 (LLM over-trust is a new concept in the IT space) IT Relevance: 13 (Directly related to LLM pipelines and deployment) Value 90 days: 15 (IT engineers and consultants can use this to improve LLM deployment within 90 days)
